claims.claim: Baur: beginners want full support (all stats, contingencies, corner cases) while veterans want bullet lists and bare-bones text with wiggle room.
claims.quote: bullet lists, bare bones text that allows them to improvise

claims.claim: Baur's writing advice to designers is to turn out a lot of prose.
claims.quote: Speed keeps you fed; quality keeps you respected.

claims.claim: Baur (ex-Dungeon editor) says most history is wasted energy; keep backstory recent and relevant and avoid openings of 'Thousands of years ago'.
claims.source: Adventure Builder: Writing Your First Adventure, Part 1 of 6 (Wolfgang Baur, Wizards.com, 2006-07-28)
claims.quote: avoid anything that starts "Thousands of years ago..."

claims.claim: The four errors Baur saw constantly at Dungeon: too much useless backstory, slow starts, random encounters, too many encounters.
claims.source: Adventure Builder: Writing Your First Adventure, Part 1 of 6 (Wolfgang Baur, Wizards.com, 2006-07-28)

claims.claim: Involved history that the PCs cannot learn belongs in sourcebooks, not adventures.
claims.source: Adventure Builder: Writing Your First Adventure, Part 1 of 6 (Wolfgang Baur, Wizards.com, 2006-07-28)

claims.claim: Hooks must be specific and hard to refuse; vague or cliched openings (stranger in a tavern, request from the mayor) fail.
claims.source: Adventure Builder: Setting the Hook, Part 2 of 6 (Wolfgang Baur, Wizards.com, 2006-08-11)
claims.quote: Vague, overused, or clichéd hooks don't interest players

claims.claim: Baur borrows fiction's inciting incident: an arrow with an Elvish note shot into camp beats a guy in a bar.
claims.source: Adventure Builder: Setting the Hook, Part 2 of 6 (Wolfgang Baur, Wizards.com, 2006-08-11)
claims.quote: In fiction, it would be called the "inciting incident."

claims.feature: design labels kept out of game text
claims.claim: Noonan deliberately used modern-sounding monster role labels (mook, artillery, decathlete) so they would not creep into published game text.
claims.source: Design & Development: How to Make a Monster Manual, Part 1 (David Noonan, 2007-07-27)
claims.quote: I didn't want the roles to creep into game text

claims.claim: Monster entries are not allowed to break across page spreads, which limits text length and illustration size.
claims.source: Design & Development: How to Make a Monster Manual, Part 1 (David Noonan, 2007-07-27)
claims.quote: monsters don't break out of page spreads

claims.claim: Rich Baker, reviewing his own TSR adventures, calls his heavy use of boxed text a 2e-era style thing.
WotC scheduled adventure writing in 'MU' units of 32 pages or 20,000-22,000 words, about one designer-month each.
WotC freelancers in 2012 were held to the Chicago Manual of Style and required to deliver manuscripts in WotC's Word templates needing minimal grammar or syntax editing.
claims.source: Freelancer Chronicles: The Coast Wizards and I, Some Lessons (Critical Hits, 2012-12-19)
claims.quote: that's going to be your main bible

claims.claim: The WotC Adventure Guide, as quoted by Shea, instructs writers to focus on the here and now and omit verbose backstories.
claims.source: On Writing Adventures (Mike Shea, Sly Flourish, 2019-06-17)
claims.quote: Focus on the here and now. Omit verbose backstories
claims.page: compilation of designer advice incl. WotC Adventure Guide

claims.claim: Kobold Guide precepts quoted by Shea: small beats large, be specific, read your work aloud.
claims.source: On Writing Adventures (Mike Shea, Sly Flourish, 2019-06-17)
claims.quote: Small beats large. Keep it brief
claims.page: compilation of designer advice incl. WotC Adventure Guide

claims.claim: Greenwood says shared-world writers must fit in, perhaps even to a particular prose style, without contradicting existing lore.
claims.source: Making the Realms Shine: A Conversation with Ed Greenwood, Part I (Kobold Press, 2009)
claims.quote: perhaps even to a particular prose style
